milestones.notes: 1.9 replaces 1.8's interpreter-scheduled green threads with real OS threads, but a single Global VM Lock (GVL) still serializes Ruby bytecode execution -- see true_parallelism

Ractor (experimental): separate Ractors run on separate OS threads without sharing the main GVL, but objects crossing Ractors must be shareable/frozen and most gems/C extensions are not Ractor-safe; Ractor's API itself was overhauled again in 4.0 (Ractor::Port)
cooperative, explicitly-resumed coroutines (Fiber class); did not exist in 1.8
Fiber::SchedulerInterface hooks blocking IO/Mutex/sleep so libraries can provide non-blocking concurrency without rewriting call sites; this is the version floor the `async` gem ecosystem requires

1.9 introduces the M17N model (every String/Regexp carries an Encoding) but still requires a `# encoding:` magic comment for non-US-ASCII source; 2.0 makes UTF-8 the default source encoding so the magic comment becomes unnecessary for UTF-8 files
RubyGems bundled with the interpreter from 1.9.1; Bundler (a separate gem since 2010) is bundled as a default gem from 2.6
2.0 added keyword arguments; 2.7 deprecated implicit Hash-to-kwargs conversion; 3.0 removes it -- one of Ruby's largest breaking changes
case/in pattern matching shipped experimental (with a warning) in 2.7 and stabilized without warning in 3.0

MJIT (2.6, shells out to a C compiler at runtime) -> YJIT (3.1, experimental) -> YJIT production-ready (3.2) -> RJIT added experimental/research-only (3.3) -> RJIT removed, ZJIT added experimental (4.0). None of these are enabled by default; YJIT needs an explicit --yjit flag through 4.0.
RBS type-signature language + bundled TypeProf inferencer; opt-in and unenforced, not a compiler-checked type system, and most gems ship no RBS signatures

depends on the openssl gem being linked against OpenSSL 1.1.1+ on the host; Ruby does not vendor OpenSSL, so actual TLS 1.3 availability tracks the system/build's OpenSSL version rather than the Ruby version alone
RubyInstaller/RubyInstaller2 x64 (mingw-w64) builds; exact first-version cutover is not separately documented by ruby-lang.org, inferred from RubyInstaller release history

no official ruby-lang.org macOS binaries at any version; Apple Silicon support means Homebrew/rbenv/ruby-build building natively rather than under Rosetta 2, which solidified around the 2.7/3.0 era alongside Homebrew's own arm64 rollout
RubyInstaller2 arm64 Windows builds are recent and experimental; exact introduction version is not confirmed against an official changelog here

os_support.windows: One-Click Installer (mswin32/mingw32 builds); targeted Windows 2000/XP-era Windows
os_support.macos: Source build; Fink/MacPorts packages; PowerPC and early Intel Macs, no arm64
os_support.linux: Source build or distro packages; any glibc Linux

added: Blocks, mixins and the core object model later versions build on
$KCODE-based multi-byte string handling (not per-string encoding objects)
In-process green-thread concurrency (Thread scheduled entirely by the interpreter, no OS threads)
limitations: Green threads only: the interpreter schedules Thread objects itself, so one blocking syscall (e.g. a slow read()) stalls every Ruby thread in the process -- fixed by native threads in 1.9
No Fiber class (added 1.9)
No per-string Encoding objects; text handling relies on the global $KCODE variable and byte-oriented String methods -- fixed by the M17N model in 1.9
No keyword arguments; APIs fake them with a trailing Hash argument (real keyword args added in 2.0)
RubyGems not included in the interpreter; installed separately (bundled from 1.9.1)
No Bundler (didn't exist yet; released 2010, bundled with Ruby from 2.6)

os_support.windows: One-Click Installer continued (mswin32/mingw32); no official x64 builds
os_support.macos: Source build; Apple bundled 1.8 as system Ruby throughout this era, so 1.9 was mostly self-installed via source/MacPorts/rvm

added: YARV bytecode VM replaces the old tree-walking MRI interpreter
Native OS threads, still serialized by a Global VM Lock (GVL) -- only one thread runs Ruby code at a time
Fiber class: cooperative, explicitly-resumed coroutines
M17N encoding model: every String/Regexp carries an Encoding
RubyGems bundled with the interpreter from 1.9.1
limitations: Threads are native but still run one at a time under the GVL -- no true CPU parallelism for Ruby code (Ractor arrives 3.0, and even then only across Ractors)
No keyword arguments (2.0)
No refinements (2.0 experimental, 2.1 stable)
Non-ASCII source still needs a `# encoding:` magic comment; UTF-8 isn't assumed until 2.0
No Bundler bundled (external gem until 2.6)
1.8 scripts relying on $KCODE or old block-scoping rules broke outright on the 1.9 upgrade

os_support.macos: Bundled as OS X 10.9+ system Ruby (2.0.0); source build/Homebrew for other versions/OS releases

added: Keyword arguments (required and optional)
Refinements (experimental)
UTF-8 default source encoding -- no magic comment needed for UTF-8 source
Enumerable#lazy
Module#prepend
limitations: Refinements are explicitly experimental; semantics still changed through 2.1
Still GVL-bound native threads; no parallel execution of Ruby code
No Fiber scheduler / non-blocking IO integration (3.0)
No pattern matching (2.7 experimental, 3.0 stable)
No frozen_string_literal magic comment (2.3)

os_support.macos: Source build/Homebrew; not the OS X-bundled system Ruby (which stayed on 2.0.0)

added: Refinements promoted from experimental to a supported (though still discouraged-for-libraries) feature
RGenGC: generational garbage collector
Rational/Complex numeric literals (1r, 1i)
Method#parameters improvements for introspecting keyword args
limitations: Still no true parallel threads (GVL-bound)
No pattern matching
No frozen_string_literal magic comment
Keyword arguments still implicitly convertible from/to a trailing Hash -- the breaking separation is 3.0

added: Incremental garbage collector (reduces GC pause times)
Symbols are now garbage-collected, fixing the long-standing unbounded Symbol memory growth
Continued Fixnum/Bignum split (unified into Integer in 2.4)
limitations: Fixnum vs Bignum is still an implementation detail programs can observe (e.g. via #class) -- unified in 2.4
No JIT of any kind (MJIT arrives 2.6)
TLS support depends entirely on whatever OpenSSL the Ruby build links against; no guarantee of TLS 1.3 (needs OpenSSL 1.1.1, which postdates this release)

os_support.windows: Last major covered by the original one-click RubyInstaller (older MinGW toolchain) before RubyInstaller2 takes over Windows builds at 2.4

added: frozen_string_literal magic comment (opt-in, per file)
Safe navigation operator (&.)
Hash#dig / Array#dig
limitations: frozen_string_literal is opt-in per file; nothing is frozen by default (a later plan to default it to true was never shipped, including in 3.4/4.0)
No JIT, no pattern matching, no Ractor
Original RubyInstaller's older MinGW toolchain is less current than RubyInstaller2's MSYS2 base used from 2.4 on

os_support.windows: RubyInstaller2 becomes the standard Windows installer (MSYS2-based build system); the switch away from the old mingw one-click installer also ends practical Windows XP support going forward

added: Fixnum and Bignum unified into a single Integer class
Hash#transform_keys / #transform_values
Comparable#clamp
limitations: Ractor, Fiber scheduler, YJIT and pattern matching all absent

RubyInstaller2's newer MSYS2-based toolchain targets a newer Windows baseline than the installer it replaced -- exact minimum Windows version for this specific major is inferred, not confirmed against an archived RubyInstaller2 changelog

added: rescue/else usable directly inside do...end blocks without an explicit begin
Comparable#clamp(range)
openssl gem/stdlib updates that made enabling TLS 1.2 the practical default for new code
limitations: No JIT yet (2.6)
No YJIT (3.1)
TLS 1.3 needs the underlying OpenSSL to be 1.1.1+; Ruby's openssl gem doesn't vendor OpenSSL, so TLS 1.3 availability depends on how/when the interpreter was built, not the Ruby version alone

added: MJIT: experimental method-based JIT that shells out to a C compiler at runtime to compile hot methods to native code
Endless ranges ((1..))
RubyVM::AST for inspecting the parse tree
Bundler bundled as a default gem for the first time
limitations: MJIT requires a C compiler to be present on the machine at *runtime*, not just at build time -- a real constraint on minimal container images and on Windows
MJIT's compile/warmup overhead often outweighs its benefit outside numeric/game-style workloads; not a general web-app win
No YJIT (3.1); no Ractor (3.0); pattern matching still absent (2.7 experimental)

added: Pattern matching (case/in) shipped as an experimental feature (prints a warning)
Numbered block parameters (_1)
Compaction GC (GC.compact)
Deprecation warnings for implicit keyword-argument/Hash conversion, ahead of 3.0's breaking separation
limitations: Pattern matching is experimental and warns on use; its syntax still changed before stabilizing in 3.0
Keyword-argument/Hash auto-conversion still works but is deprecated -- code relying on it breaks outright in 3.0
No Ractor, no true parallelism
No Fiber scheduler / non-blocking IO integration

os_support.macos: Source build/Homebrew; Apple Silicon (arm64) support solidifying via Homebrew/rbenv/ruby-build around this release rather than as an official ruby-lang.org binary

added: Ractor (experimental): actor-style true parallelism -- separate Ractors run on separate OS threads without sharing the main GVL

Fiber Scheduler: hooks blocking calls (IO#read, Mutex#lock, Kernel#sleep, etc.) so libraries such as the `async` gem can provide non-blocking concurrency without rewriting call sites -- this is the version floor the async gem ecosystem requires
RBS type-signature language plus a bundled TypeProf type inferencer
Pattern matching stabilized (no warning)
Keyword arguments formally separated from positional/Hash arguments (breaking change)
limitations: Ractor is explicitly experimental: objects passed between Ractors must be shareable/frozen, most existing C extensions and gems are not Ractor-safe, and the main Ractor still has its own GVL
RBS/TypeProf are opt-in and unenforced -- there is no compiler-checked static typing, and most gems ship no RBS signatures
Keyword-argument separation breaks any code/gem still relying on implicit Hash-to-kwargs conversion from 2.7 and earlier -- one of the largest breaking changes in Ruby's history
Fiber Scheduler only helps code paths that go through it; C extensions doing blocking syscalls directly bypass it
The '3x3' performance goal was measured on a single-threaded benchmark (Optcarrot), not representative of typical web-app workloads

os_support.windows: RubyInstaller2 (MSYS2-based); YJIT not available here (Unix x86-64 only at this release)
os_support.macos: Source build/Homebrew; Apple Silicon (arm64) builds available via Homebrew/rbenv, but YJIT is x86-64-only so it does not run under Apple Silicon at this release
os_support.linux: Source build or distro packages; YJIT usable on x86-64

added: YJIT (experimental): Shopify's in-process JIT using basic-block versioning; disabled by default, opt-in via --yjit
Debug.gem: full debugger rewrite with remote/multi-process/multi-thread debugging and VS Code/Chrome DevTools integration
error_highlight gem: precise error-location underlining in backtraces
Hash/keyword value omission shorthand ({x:})
limitations: YJIT at launch only supports Unix-like x86-64 -- no Windows, no arm64/Apple Silicon, no other CPU architectures
YJIT is off by default and still experimental; needs an explicit flag and extra memory for compiled code
Ractor still experimental with the same shareability constraints as 3.0
No default-on JIT of any kind for typical deployments

os_support.macos: Source build/Homebrew; Apple Silicon (arm64) well-supported via community builds, still no official ruby-lang.org binary
os_support.linux: Source build or distro packages; plus an experimental WASI/WebAssembly build (ruby.wasm) for running Ruby in browsers/WASI runtimes

added: YJIT declared production-ready / stable enough for general use (still opt-in, off by default)
WASI-based WebAssembly build (experimental, ruby.wasm)
Data.define lightweight value-object class
Anonymous block forwarding (def foo(&); bar(&); end)
Improved OpenSSL 3.x compatibility in the openssl gem
limitations: YJIT is production-ready but still requires an explicit --yjit flag; not on by default
The WASM/WASI build has no real OS threads, no TCP sockets, and a cut-down stdlib -- most gems with C extensions can't run there
Ractor still experimental; its API kept changing (overhauled again in 4.0)
Apple Silicon (arm64 macOS) support remains community-provided (Homebrew, rbenv/ruby-build); ruby-lang.org still ships no official macOS binaries at all

os_support.macos: Source build/Homebrew; Apple Silicon well-supported via community builds
os_support.linux: Source build or distro packages; WASI/WebAssembly build continues

added: Prism parser bundled as a default gem (opt-in via --parser=prism): a portable, error-tolerant recursive-descent parser meant to eventually replace the parse.y-based parser
RJIT: a new pure-Ruby JIT (replacing MJIT) built for experimentation/research, not production
YJIT: reported >3x faster than the interpreter on Optcarrot; code GC disabled by default; runtime-toggleable via RubyVM::YJIT.enable
M:N thread scheduler (opt-in via RUBY_MN_THREADS=1): multiple Ruby Threads multiplexed onto fewer OS threads
limitations: Prism is bundled but not yet the default parser -- you must pass --parser=prism to use it (default parser switch is 3.4)
RJIT is explicitly documented as experimental/research-only, x86-64 Unix only, and slower than YJIT -- not a production JIT choice
M:N thread scheduler is opt-in and disabled by default on the main Ractor for C-extension compatibility
Ractor API still not finalized (replaced again in 4.0's Ractor::Port)

os_support.windows: RubyInstaller2 (MSYS2-based); early/experimental arm64 Windows builds begin appearing around this era
os_support.macos: Source build/Homebrew; Apple Silicon well-supported via community builds
os_support.linux: Source build or distro packages; WASI/WebAssembly build continues

added: Prism becomes the default parser for CRuby (the old parse.y-based parser remains available as a fallback)
`it` as an implicit single-block-parameter reference, alongside numbered params
'Happy Eyeballs' Version 2 enabled by default for hostname resolution (races IPv4/IPv6 connections in Socket/TCPSocket)
Warnings added around frozen-string-literal-adjacent mutation as ecosystem prep work, without flipping the file-level default
limitations: The long-floated plan to make string literals frozen by default was NOT shipped in 3.4 (nor in 4.0) after ecosystem pushback -- frozen_string_literal remains opt-in, magic-comment only
YJIT remains opt-in (not on by default)
Ractor API instability continues; the bigger overhaul lands in 4.0
RJIT still present but slated for removal (removed in 4.0)

os_support.windows: RubyInstaller2 (MSYS2-based); building/using 4.0 on Windows requires MSVC 14.0+ (Visual Studio 2015 or later) -- older MSVC toolchains are unsupported
os_support.macos: Source build/Homebrew; Apple Silicon well-supported via community builds, still no official ruby-lang.org binary
os_support.linux: Source build or distro packages; WASI/WebAssembly build continues

added: Ruby Box (experimental, RUBY_BOX=1): isolates constants/monkey-patches/loaded libraries between 'boxes' in one process, aimed at test isolation and blue-green deploys
ZJIT: a next-generation JIT written in Rust (building Ruby itself now needs Rust 1.85.0+); currently faster than the plain interpreter but slower than YJIT
Ractor::Port replaces the old Ractor message-passing API
Pathname promoted from a default gem to a core class; Set promoted from autoloaded stdlib to a core class
limitations: ZJIT is explicitly not production-ready; YJIT remains the production JIT choice
The Ractor rewrite is a breaking change: Ractor.yield, Ractor#take, Ractor#close_incoming and Ractor#close_outgoing are all removed in favor of Ractor::Port -- 3.x Ractor code needs porting
RJIT removed entirely (--rjit flag gone)
CGI library gutted to just cgi/escape; SortedSet removed from the standard library (now needs a separate gem)
Kernel#open/IO.popen-style process spawning via a leading '|' argument removed; Process::Status#& and #>> removed
Building Ruby itself now requires a Rust toolchain (for ZJIT) in addition to a C compiler -- a new build dependency versus every prior major
Ruby Box and ZJIT are both experimental/opt-in -- the default single-namespace, YJIT-or-interpreter execution model is unchanged
